Foundations: Writing the Standard Your Product Must Meet

You turn a product that lives in your hands and memory into a written specification with measured quantities and tolerances. You score how ready you are for the buyer you want, and you learn change control, the habit that lets you improve the product without letting it drift.
From 'my way' to a written specification with tolerances
Explain the difference between a recipe, a specification and a standard
Convert cup, handful and spoon measures into grams using a kitchen scale
Set a sensible tolerance for each ingredient and for the finished pack

A buyer who has never met you cannot taste your care or watch your hands. What she can check is whether every pack is the same as the last one, and whether you can show on paper what "the same" means. That written description is your **product specification**, often shortened to **spec**. When you make every batch to it, and check that you did, your product becomes **standardised**.

Three words are easy to mix up, so fix them now. A **recipe or formula** lists what goes in and how much. A **specification** goes further: it adds the process steps, the conditions (time, heat, order), the packaging and a description of the finished product, with numbers wherever possible. A **standard** is a document that a group agrees everyone must meet, such as a Nigerian Industrial Standard published by the Standards Organisation of Nigeria (SON), or a buyer's own requirements. Your spec is your house standard.
A balance scale
Standardising starts with replacing cups and handfuls with weights you can repeat.
Why cups and handfuls fail

A cup of ground pepper packed down holds more than a cup poured loosely. A heaped spoon of salt changes with whoever is holding the spoon. Volume measures also change with how fine the grind is and how damp the ingredient is. **Weight does not care who is measuring.** A digital kitchen scale that reads to 1 gram costs far less than one rejected order, and it is the single most useful tool in this course.
Worked example: turning a yaji recipe into grams

For example, Hauwa in Kaduna sells suya spice (yaji) in 100 g pouches. Her recipe was "4 cups groundnut powder, 2 cups pepper, ginger, garlic, onion powder and 2 heaped spoons of salt". Customers said some packs were too salty.
She weighs each ingredient three times as she normally measures it. Her cup of groundnut powder averages 150 g, so 4 cups is 600 g. Her cup of pepper averages 100 g, so 2 cups is 200 g.
Her two heaped spoons of salt weigh 46 g, 55 g and 49 g on three tries. The average is (46 + 55 + 49) / 3 = 50 g, but the spread is 55 minus 46 = 9 g. That spread is why some packs tasted saltier.
She weighs the other ingredients the same way: ginger 80 g, garlic 40 g, onion powder 30 g.
She adds up the batch: 600 + 200 + 80 + 40 + 50 + 30 = 1,000 g. A 1 kg batch is easy to scale: a 3 kg batch is simply every number times 3.
She writes the formula in grams with a tolerance of plus or minus 5 g per ingredient for a 1 kg batch, and plus or minus 2 g for salt, because salt affects taste most.

Hauwa's spec now says 1,000 g batch: groundnut powder 600 g, pepper 200 g, ginger 80 g, salt 50 g (plus or minus 2 g), garlic 40 g, onion powder 30 g. The salty-pack complaints stop because salt is no longer measured by spoon.

Tolerances: how much difference is allowed

No two batches are identical to the gram. A **tolerance** is the honest allowed range, written as a target plus or minus an amount. Set tighter tolerances for things that change safety, taste or the label (salt, preservatives, net weight) and looser ones for things that matter less. If you cannot measure a quality with a number, describe it in words and keep a reference: a sealed **reference sample** from a batch you were happy with, a photo, or a colour card. When you are unsure, you compare against the reference, not your memory.
The four layers of rules
Laws and regulator requirements
National standards (NIS from SON)
Buyer requirements
Your house specification
Your house spec sits at the base and must satisfy every layer above it that applies to your product.

Read the pyramid from the top. **Laws and regulators** come first: in Nigeria, NAFDAC regulates food, cosmetics, drugs, chemicals and similar products, and SON is responsible for standards for many other products. **National standards** describe minimum quality for a product type and are available from SON. **Buyers** such as supermarkets or hotels may add their own rules. Your house spec is where you write down how you meet all of these, plus your own quality choices.
Write the real recipe first

Write the spec for the product you actually make today, not an ideal one. If you secretly add more pepper when customers complain, write that down too, then decide properly. A spec that does not match reality is worse than none, because people will trust it.
Food hygiene comes with the spec

For food, build the WHO Five Keys to Safer Food into your process steps: keep clean, separate raw and cooked, cook thoroughly, keep food at safe temperatures, and use safe water and raw materials. For groundnut products, reject any nuts that look mouldy, shrivelled or discoloured.

Standardisation has a cost in time and money, so do it in the order your market demands. A woman selling to neighbours on WhatsApp, a woman supplying a supermarket and a woman tendering for a hotel contract need different paperwork. The skill in this lesson is to see exactly which gaps stand between you and your next buyer, and to fix those first.

Worked example: tote bags for a hotel gift shop
For example, Chioma in Aba sews ankara tote bags. A hotel gift shop asks for 200 bags per quarter, all one size, each with a care label, delivered with an invoice.
She scores herself: spec 1, templates 2, materials and backup supplier 1, label 0, records 0, finished check 1, packaging 1, capacity 1.
She checks capacity: 200 bags over a 13-week quarter is 200 / 13 = about 15.4 bags a week. She makes about 25 a week, so volume is possible, but only if her other orders leave room.
She ranks gaps by what the hotel cares about. Care labels and same size are stated requirements, so the label (0) and spec (1) are urgent. Records (0) matter for invoicing and repeat orders.
She plans: finish the spec with exact measurements this week, order care labels next, and start an order record book before the first delivery.
Instead of feeling "not ready", Chioma has three named gaps in priority order and knows the volume is within her capacity.

Business model questions to answer honestly
Will this buyer pay on delivery, or after 30 or more days? Can your cash carry the materials until then?
Does the order price cover the extra costs of labels, records and inspection time?
If the buyer doubles the order, can you still meet your own spec, or will quality slip?
Is this buyer a step towards a bigger channel, or a one-off?
Score with a second person
Ask a trusted helper or another producer to score you as well. We all rate our own work kindly. Where your scores differ by more than 1 point, look again with fresh eyes.
Readiness is not the same as quality

A producer can make an excellent product and still score low on readiness, because readiness measures whether the quality is written down, repeatable and provable. The reverse also happens: neat paperwork around a product customers do not like. Keep both in view. Before you spend on documents, confirm that buyers in your target channel actually want the product, for example by a small trial sale or by asking the buyer for feedback on a sample. Then use the scorecard to make that good product dependable. Repeat the scorecard every three months; a rising score is a simple, honest measure of progress you can show a business adviser or lender.
Do not promise what you cannot show

If a buyer asks for registration, a test report or a certificate you do not have, say so and give a realistic date. Claiming a registration you do not hold is illegal and ends trust instantly when checked.

Change control: improving the product without letting it drift
Explain why unplanned small changes destroy consistency
Run a side-by-side trial batch before changing the spec
Update the spec version, label and team training after an approved change
Recognise changes that may need a regulator's approval

Most products do not change in one big step. They **drift**: a little more of this because the new supplier's pepper is milder, a slightly bigger handle because the worker prefers it, a different jar because it was cheaper this month. After six months the product on the shelf no longer matches the sample the buyer approved. **Change control** is the simple discipline that stops drift: no change to the product, its materials or its package goes into production until it has been tested, approved and written into a new version of the spec.
Two versions being compared side by side
Test the old and new versions side by side before you change the spec.
What counts as a change
A new supplier or grade of any material, even if it has the same name
Any change in quantity, process step, time or temperature
A new container, closure, pouch or label
A new machine or tool that does a step differently
A new person doing a critical step for the first time
The change control path
Propose change in writing
Run side-by-side trial
Compare against the spec
Approve and update version
Retrain and relabel
Every change follows the same five steps before it reaches a customer.

Keep a **change log** at the back of your spec file: date, what changed, why, the trial result, who approved it, and the new version number. Use simple numbering. A small change moves 1.0 to 1.1. A big change, such as a new main ingredient, moves 1.1 to 2.0. Remove or clearly mark old copies of the spec so nobody works from the wrong one.
Worked example: a hotter pepper from a new supplier

For example, Hauwa's usual pepper seller in Kaduna runs out, and the new supplier's ground pepper is noticeably hotter. Her spec (version 1.0) uses 200 g pepper and 600 g groundnut powder per 1 kg batch.
She writes the proposal: new pepper supplier, reduce pepper and increase groundnut powder to keep heat and weight the same.
She makes two small trial batches on the same day: one with the old pepper at 200 g per kg (the control), and one with the new pepper at 170 g per kg and groundnut powder at 630 g per kg.
She checks the new formula adds up: 630 + 170 + 80 + 40 + 50 + 30 = 1,000 g.
She asks 10 regular customers to taste both, unlabelled. 7 say they cannot tell the difference or prefer the new one.
She checks the label: ingredients by weight are still groundnut powder, pepper, ginger, salt, garlic, onion powder, so the order on the label does not change. Net weight stays 100 g.
She records the change as version 1.1, files the trial notes and shows her packer the new weights.
The product stays consistent for customers even though the raw material changed, and Hauwa has a dated record that explains why her spec says 170 g.
Changes that touch the label or the law

Some changes reach beyond your kitchen. If the order of ingredients by weight changes, the ingredient list on the label must change. If you add an ingredient that is a known allergen, such as groundnut, wheat, milk, egg or soy, it must be declared. If your product is registered with NAFDAC, check with NAFDAC before changing the formula, pack size or label of the registered product, because the registration relates to the product as it was approved. Treat this as a change control step, not an afterthought.
One change at a time
If you change the pepper and the mixing time together and the taste changes, you cannot know which caused it. Change one thing per trial whenever you can.
Leading the discipline

Your team will copy what you do. If you add "a little extra" when you are in a hurry, they will too. Say clearly that ideas for improvement are welcome, and that the way to use an idea is to bring it to you for a trial, not to try it on a customer's order. When a trial succeeds, give credit to the person who suggested it. That keeps creativity alive while the product stays the same.

Good change control also covers your packaging suppliers. If the printer changes the label paper, or the jar seller offers a different lid, ask for a sample first and test it with your product: does the label stay on when the pouch is handled with oily fingers, does the lid seal without leaking when the jar lies on its side for a day? A packaging change that fails in a customer's bag costs far more than the small saving that tempted you. Record packaging trials in the same change log as formula changes, so the history of the whole product sits in one place.
Keep the old reference sample
When you approve a new version, keep one sealed sample of the last batch of the old version as well. If a buyer later says "this is different", you can compare honestly.
Drift is many small unrecorded changes; change control stops it.

Systems, Quality and Operations

You write standard operating procedures that work without you in the room, check that every label tells the truth and every pack holds what it says, and put a naira figure on the cost of poor quality so you can decide what to fix first.
Writing SOPs that work when you are not in the room
Describe the parts of a one-page standard operating procedure (SOP)
Write numbered steps with built-in checkpoints and records
Include the correct safety precautions for heat and hot oil
Test an SOP by having someone else follow it

Your specification says **what** the product must be. A **standard operating procedure (SOP)** says **how** to do one task so that it comes out right every time, whoever does it. A small business usually needs only a handful: receiving materials, making a batch, filling and sealing, labelling and coding, cleaning, and final inspection. Each one should fit on a single page that can be stuck on the wall or saved as a photo on a worker's phone.
A woman ticking off a task list
A good SOP is a short list of steps anyone can follow and tick off.
Parts of a one-page SOP
Title, number and version
Purpose and when to use
Materials, tools and safety
Numbered steps with checkpoints
Record to fill in
Approved by and date
If any of these six parts is missing, the SOP will be followed differently by different people.
Rules for writing steps
Start each step with an action verb: weigh, pour, wipe, seal, check, record.
Put one action in each step. "Fill and cap and label" is three steps.
Use numbers, not feelings: "102 g on the scale", not "fill well".
Mark **checkpoints** where the worker must stop and check before going on, and say what to do if the check fails.
Say which record to fill in and when, so the paperwork is part of the job, not an extra.
Use the words your workers use. If everyone calls the double boiler "the pot inside pot", write both.
Worked example: SOP for filling hair pomade jars

For example, Funmi in Ibadan makes an oil-based hair pomade in 100 g jars. Two helpers fill jars, and the jar weights vary. She writes SOP-03, version 1.0, using her own house rule of a 102 g fill target so that no jar falls below the 100 g on the label.
Purpose: fill, cap and code 100 g jars from one melted batch. Use for every batch.

Materials and tools: clean dry jars and lids, digital scale reading to 1 g, jug with spout, clean cloth, batch code stamp, batch record sheet. Safety: heat-resistant gloves, long sleeves, lid for the pot within reach.
Step 1: Check the scale with the 100 g test weight. It must read 100 g. If not, stop and tell Funmi.
Step 2: Place an empty jar on the scale and press tare so it reads 0 g.
Step 3: Pour the melted pomade until the scale reads 102 g. Acceptable range: 101 g to 104 g.
Step 4: Checkpoint: weigh every 10th jar again after it sets a little. If any jar is below 101 g, top it up and tell Funmi.
Step 5: Wipe the rim, close the lid, and stamp the batch code on the base.
Step 6: Leave jars upright to set fully before packing. Record the number of jars filled and any rejects on the batch sheet.
Both helpers now fill to the same weight, every 10th jar is checked, and the batch sheet shows how many jars each batch gave. Funmi can travel for a day and the work still comes out the same.
Hot oil and wax safety

Melt oils and waxes in a double boiler or on low heat, never leave the pot unattended, and keep children and pets out of the work area. Wear heat-resistant gloves and long sleeves. If oil catches fire, turn off the heat and cover the pot with a lid or fire blanket. Never pour water on burning oil, it makes the fire spread violently. Cool a burn under clean running water and seek medical help for serious burns.
The newcomer test

An SOP is only finished when someone who has never done the task can follow it and get the right result. Give the page to a helper or family member, say nothing, and watch. Every time they hesitate, ask a question or do something you did not expect, the SOP needs a clearer step. Rewrite, then test again. Two rounds usually catch most gaps.
Where SOPs live

Keep a master copy in a folder (paper or a shared Google Drive folder) with a simple index: SOP number, title, version, date. Put a laminated or plastic-sleeved copy at the place where the work is done. When a version changes through change control, collect and destroy the old copy at the workstation the same day. Two different versions on the wall is how mistakes start.

A label is a promise. It promises what is inside, how much, who made it and how long it stays good. Standardisation means the promise is checked, not hoped for. In this lesson you check two things on every batch: that the **label matches the spec**, and that the **pack holds at least what the label says**.
A product label tag
Every word and number on your label should trace back to your spec and your records.
What a prepackaged food label must show

The **Codex General Standard for the Labelling of Prepackaged Foods**, agreed by FAO and WHO member countries, is the reference many national food rules build on. Its mandatory items are below. NAFDAC's own labelling rules for Nigeria apply to products sold here, so confirm the details with NAFDAC for your product, but this list is the right starting point for any food label check.

Codex also sets how the date is written: day and month for products that last up to three months, month and year for longer ones. The date must come from evidence, such as a shelf-life test you recorded, not from a guess or a competitor's label. Known allergens such as groundnut, milk, egg, wheat and soy should be easy to see on the label, because for some people they are dangerous.
Never print a number you do not hold

Only print a NAFDAC registration number that NAFDAC has issued for that exact product. Words like "NAFDAC approved" or "SON certified" on a product that is not registered or certified are false claims and can lead to seizure and prosecution.
Step one: check the scale

A weight check is only as good as the scale. Before each session, place a known **test weight** (a certified 100 g or 500 g weight, bought from a scale supplier) on the scale. If the reading is off, the scale must be re-zeroed, recalibrated using the maker's instructions, or replaced. Never use a product pack as a test weight; its true weight is exactly what you are trying to find out.
Step two: sample and weigh

For a small batch, weigh 10 packs picked from the start, middle and end of filling, not the 10 nearest your hand. Write down every weight, then calculate the **average** (add them and divide by 10) and find the **lowest** pack. Many producers use two house rules: the average must be at least the declared weight, and no single pack may fall below a set lower limit. Official tolerances for net quantity are set by law, so ask the regulator what applies to your product and make your house rules at least as strict.
Worked example: a scale that reads 1 g high

For example, Hauwa checks a batch of 100 g yaji pouches. Her house rules: average at least 100.0 g, no pouch below 98.0 g. She weighs 10 pouches before checking her scale: 101.2, 100.4, 99.1, 102.0, 100.8, 98.6, 101.5, 100.9, 99.7 and 101.0 g.
She adds them: 1,005.2 g. Average = 1,005.2 / 10 = 100.52 g. Lowest = 98.6 g. Both rules seem to pass.
Then she places her 100 g test weight on the scale. It reads 101 g. The scale reads 1 g too high.
She subtracts 1 g from every reading. The true average is 100.52 minus 1 = 99.52 g, and the lowest pouch is really 97.6 g.
Result against her rules: average 99.52 g is below 100.0 g (fail), and one pouch at 97.6 g is below 98.0 g (fail).
She holds the batch, recalibrates the scale, reweighs and tops up every pouch that is below 100 g, then raises her fill target to 101 g so the average sits safely above 100 g.
She records the problem, the fix and the new target on the batch sheet and updates SOP-03.
Without the test weight, Hauwa would have released an underweight batch while her records said it passed. Checking the scale first turned a hidden failure into a recorded correction.
The weight-check cycle
Verify scale with test weight
Sample packs across the batch
Record every weight
Compare to house rules
Correct, record and adjust
Run the cycle every batch; the record is your proof of honest quantity.
Non-food products

The same thinking applies beyond food. A cosmetic jar should state its contents honestly and list ingredients. A garment or bag should carry fibre content and care instructions; the international care symbols use a washtub for washing, a triangle for bleaching, a square for drying, an iron for ironing and a circle for professional cleaning. Whatever the product, every claim on the label, including "handmade", "100% cotton" or "natural", must be something you can prove from your spec and supplier records.
Check the label against the spec: name, ingredients by weight, net contents, address, batch code, date.
Verify the scale with a test weight before trusting any weight check.
Sample across the batch, record every weight, and check both the average and the lowest pack.
A failed check means hold, correct, record and adjust the process, not just repack quietly.

Standardisation is not free: labels, templates, test weights and inspection time all cost money. But poor quality also costs money, it is just hidden in thread used twice, materials thrown away and refunds. Quality managers call the total of these the **cost of quality**. When you add it up honestly, you usually find that spending a little on prevention saves a lot on failures.

For example, Chioma makes about 200 ankara tote bags a month and sells them at about 8,000 naira each (approximate, illustrative figures). Before standardising, sizes vary because she cuts by eye.
Before: 15% need rework, which is 30 bags. Each rework costs about 700 naira in labour and thread: 30 x 700 = 21,000 naira.
5% are scrapped, which is 10 bags. Each scrapped bag lost about 3,500 naira of material and labour: 10 x 3,500 = 35,000 naira.
4 bags a month come back for refund at 8,000 naira: 4 x 8,000 = 32,000 naira.
Failure cost before = 21,000 + 35,000 + 32,000 = 88,000 naira a month, with almost no prevention spending.

After: she buys cutting templates for about 45,000 naira, spread over 6 months = 7,500 naira a month. Inspection takes 10 hours a month at 1,000 naira an hour = 10,000 naira. Care labels cost about 60 naira x 200 = 12,000 naira. Prevention and checking = 7,500 + 10,000 + 12,000 = 29,500 naira.
Failures fall to 4% rework (8 bags x 700 = 5,600), 1% scrap (2 bags x 3,500 = 7,000) and 1 refund (8,000): 5,600 + 7,000 + 8,000 = 20,600 naira.
Total after = 29,500 + 20,600 = 50,100 naira. Saving = 88,000 minus 50,100 = 37,900 naira a month.
Quality cost per bag falls from 88,000 / 200 = 440 naira to 50,100 / 200 = about 251 naira, and fewer unhappy customers means more repeat orders on top.

Pricing compliance into every unit

Ongoing costs such as labels, inspection time and record books belong in your unit cost every month, not only in the month you started. One-off costs such as templates, a test weight, a label redesign or a registration should be spread over the months or units they serve. Then you can judge a one-off cost with a simple **payback question**: how many extra sales must it unlock to pay for itself?
Write the one-off cost, for example a label redesign and new printing plates at about 60,000 naira (illustrative).
Write the profit you keep from each extra unit sold, for example 250 naira per yaji pouch.
Divide: 60,000 / 250 = 240 pouches.
Ask: is the new buyer likely to take at least 240 pouches within a reasonable time? If yes, the cost is justified. If not, delay it.
Capacity: checks take time

Inspection and records take real minutes. If final inspection takes 3 minutes a bag, 200 bags need 600 minutes, which is 10 hours a month. Put that time in your weekly plan. When an order is bigger than your capacity including checks, the honest answer is a later delivery date or a smaller first order, not skipping the checks.
Track it for three months
Keep a simple tally of reworks, scraps and returns for three months. The numbers will show you exactly which fault costs most, and that is where your next prevention spending should go.
Where to spend first

Look at your four types of cost together. If external failures are high, your first spending should usually be on checking, so that faulty units stop reaching customers while you work on the cause. Once fewer faults escape, move spending upstream into prevention: better templates, clearer SOPs, training and better materials. Prevention is cheaper in the long run because it stops the fault being made at all, while checking only finds it after the time and material are spent. The goal is not zero spending on checks, but a steady shift from paying for failures to paying for doing it right the first time.

Sign off on numbers, not feelings

Decide a sign-off rule for each task before training starts, so it is fair and clear. For a production task, a common approach is a run of consecutive batches that meet the spec. Write it into the SOP so every learner knows the target.
Worked example: signing Amina off on handles

For example, Chioma's rule for handle attachment is: three batches of 10 bags in a row, each with no more than 1 bag needing rework, checked against the handle spec (length 60 cm plus or minus 1 cm, stitched 4 cm into the bag, double row).
Amina's first four batches have 3, 1, 0 and 1 handles needing rework.
Batch 1: 3 out of 10 = 30% rework, which is above the rule, so the count restarts.
Batches 2, 3 and 4: 1, 0 and 1 out of 10, each within the rule. That is three in a row.
Over those three batches she made 30 bags with 2 reworks: 2 / 30 = about 6.7%.
Chioma signs and dates Amina's line on the matrix, moving her from level 1 to level 2, and notes a refresher check in three months.
Amina is signed off on evidence she can see herself, and Chioma has a dated record to show a buyer how she trains staff.
The stop rule

Write one clear sentence and say it often: **"If anything does not match the spec, stop, set it aside and tell me. You will never be blamed for stopping."** Examples: a material that smells or looks different, a scale that fails its test weight check, a label roll with the wrong batch format. Thank the person who stops a batch, even if it turns out fine. If people fear blame, they hide problems, and hidden problems reach customers.
Teaching records, not just skills

Records are the part of the job most likely to be skipped or filled in at the end of the day from memory. Explain why each record matters, in one line: "This weight sheet is our proof to the supermarket that every jar is full." Show a correctly completed sheet as the model. Check records daily at first, and correct gently but immediately: an entry made from memory is not evidence.
Train the safety steps first

Where the work involves hot oil, sharp cutting tools, sewing machines or cleaning chemicals, train and sign off the safety steps before the production steps. A learner should know where the lid, first aid box and exit are before she touches the pot.
Refresher checks and new tasks

Skills fade and habits slip, especially after a busy season. Plan a short refresher check for every signed-off person, for example every three months: watch her do the task once against the SOP and check the last few batch records she filled. If results have slipped, move her back to level 1 for that task until she meets the sign-off rule again, and treat it as normal, not as punishment. Whenever an SOP changes through change control, everyone signed off on that task needs a quick retraining on the new version, recorded on the matrix with the date. Aim to have at least two people at level 2 on every critical task, so that one person's illness or travel never stops production or lowers quality.

When you hire someone new, start her on tasks where mistakes are easy to catch, such as packing and labelling under supervision, before moving to tasks such as formula weighing where errors are harder to see in the finished product.
Use short video notes

Record a short phone video of a correct task (no faces needed) and share it in your staff WhatsApp group. Learners can watch it again before a shift, and it uses less data than a long explanation call.

An **internal audit** is you, or someone you trust, checking whether what your documents say is what actually happens. It is the habit behind quality systems such as ISO 9001, the international standard for quality management systems, which is built on principles like customer focus, a process approach and continual improvement. You do not need ISO certification to borrow the habit. A two-hour audit every quarter keeps your standards alive and gives you honest evidence for buyers.
A person reviewing a large checklist

How to run a two-hour audit
Pick one product and gather its spec, SOPs, label, last month's batch records and the skills matrix.
Watch one batch being made without helping. Note every place where practice differs from the SOP.
Pick three finished units at random and check them against the spec: weight, appearance, label, batch code.
Trace one batch backwards: from a sold unit's batch code to the batch record to the materials used. Note any break in the chain.
Score each audit area 0, 1 or 2 and write one sentence of evidence for each score.

For example, Funmi audits her hair pomade across eight areas, scoring each 0 (missing), 1 (partly working) or 2 (working with evidence).

Scale checked before use: 2. Test weight log signed every day.
Label correct and complete: 1. Batch code is stamped on the base but the label has no best before date.
Batch records complete: 1. Two batches last month have no fill weights recorded.
Traceability: 0. A jar from a customer complaint could not be matched to its materials because supplier batch numbers were not written down.
Retained samples: 0. None kept.
Training and sign-off: 2. Matrix up to date.

A **mock recall** is a practice run. You pretend a batch is faulty and see how quickly you can find which materials went into it and who bought it. Reads to 1 gram
Same for every person
Cheaper than one rejected order
A cup of ground pepper packed down holds more than a cup poured loosely. A heaped spoon of salt changes with whoever holds the spoon.
Weight does not care who is measuring. A digital kitchen scale that reads to 1 gram costs far less than one rejected order. It is the most useful tool in this course.

Hauwa turns yaji into grams

Every number needs a tolerance: tighter where taste or safety depend.
For example, Hauwa in Kaduna sells suya spice, yaji, in 100 g pouches. Customers said some packs were too salty. So she weighed each ingredient three times, the way she normally measures.
Her two heaped spoons of salt weighed 46, 55 and 49 grams.
The average is 50 grams, but the spread is 9 grams. That spread is why some packs tasted saltier.
Groundnut powder 600 grams, pepper 200, ginger 80, salt 50, garlic 40 and onion powder 30. That is a 1,000 gram batch, easy to scale.
A tolerance is the honest allowed range. She allows plus or minus 5 grams per ingredient, but only plus or minus 2 grams for salt, because salt affects taste most. The salty-pack complaints stopped.

Six sections of a specification
Identity: name, size, version, date
Materials and approved suppliers
Formula with tolerances
Process steps and conditions
Finished product description
Packaging, label and batch code
Write six sections. Identity: the product name, size, spec number, version and date. Then each material, its grade and approved supplier.
The formula, with a tolerance beside every quantity. And the process steps in order, with time, heat or mixing conditions.
Describe the finished product: appearance, smell, taste, texture and weight. Then packaging, label version and batch code.
Keep a sealed reference sample from a good batch, and compare against it, not your memory. And write the recipe you really make today.
Safety first
Food safety belongs in the spec
Keep clean, separate raw and cooked, cook thoroughly, safe temperatures, safe water and raw materials.
For groundnut products, reject nuts that look mouldy, shrivelled or discoloured.
Declare allergens like groundnut, wheat, milk, egg or soy. Check with NAFDAC before changing a registered product.
For food, build the WHO Five Keys to Safer Food into your process steps. Keep clean, separate raw and cooked, cook thoroughly, keep food at safe temperatures, and use safe water and raw materials.
For groundnut products, reject any nuts that look mouldy, shrivelled or discoloured.
Known allergens, such as groundnut, wheat, milk, egg or soy, must be declared. If your product is registered with NAFDAC, check with NAFDAC before changing its formula, pack size or label.

Change control
Improve without drifting
Propose the change in writing
Run a side-by-side trial
Approve and update the version
Products drift through small unrecorded changes. Change control stops that. For example, Hauwa's new pepper supplier sells hotter pepper. She writes a proposal.
She makes two trial batches the same day: the old pepper at 200 grams, and the new at 170 grams, with groundnut powder raised to 630.
10 regular customers taste both, unlabelled. 7 cannot tell the difference or prefer the new one.
The label order stays the same, so she records version 1.1 in her change log.
Then she shows her packer the new weights. Change one thing at a time, and keep a sealed sample of the old version.

Your spec says what the product must be. A standard operating procedure, or SOP, says how to do one task so it comes out right, whoever does it.
A label is a promise: what is inside, how much, who made it, and how long it stays good.
So you check that every pack holds what the label says.
And you put a naira figure on poor quality, so you know what to fix first.
Worked example
Funmi's SOP for filling jars
Check the scale with the 100 g weight
Place a jar and press tare
Pour to 102 g; accept 101 g to 104 g
Checkpoint: reweigh every 10th jar
Wipe, close, stamp the batch code
Record jars filled and rejects

For example, Funmi in Ibadan makes hair pomade in 100 g jars, and two helpers fill them. Her SOP, version 1.0, fits on one page. Step one: check the scale with the 100 gram test weight. If it does not read 100, stop.
Place an empty jar on the scale and press tare, so it reads zero.
Pour until the scale reads 102 grams. Her house target is above 100 so no jar falls below the label.
A checkpoint: reweigh every 10th jar. If any is below 101 grams, top it up and tell Funmi.
Wipe the rim, close the lid, and stamp the batch code.
Record the jars filled and any rejects. Notice: one action per step, numbers instead of feelings. Then give it to a newcomer and watch. Every hesitation means a step needs rewriting.
Safety first
Use a double boiler or low heat. Never leave the pot. Children and pets out. Gloves and long sleeves.
Turn off the heat and cover the pot with a lid or fire blanket. Never pour water on burning oil.
Cool a burn under clean running water. Seek medical help for serious burns.
Safety belongs inside the SOP. Melt oils and waxes in a double boiler or on low heat, and never leave the pot. Keep children and pets out, and wear heat-resistant gloves and long sleeves.
If oil catches fire, turn off the heat and cover the pot with a lid or fire blanket. Never pour water on burning oil. It makes the fire spread violently.
Cool a burn under clean running water, and seek medical help for serious burns.
True labels
Check the label against the spec
Name that shows what the food is
Ingredients, heaviest first
Net contents in metric units
Batch code
Best before date and storage

The Codex labelling standard is a good starting point, and NAFDAC's rules apply in Nigeria. Check the name, ingredients heaviest first, net contents, your name and address, a batch code, and a best before date that comes from evidence, not a guess.
Make allergens such as groundnut, milk, egg, wheat and soy easy to see. And never print a NAFDAC number, or words like SON certified, that you do not hold.
True weights
Hauwa's scale reads 1 g high
10 pouches average 100.52 g, lowest 98.6 g
Test weight reads 101 g
True average 99.52 g, lowest 97.6 g
Hold, recalibrate, top up, target 101 g
Check the scale with a test weight before any weight check.
Hauwa's rules: average at least 100 grams, no pouch below 98. She weighs 10 pouches from the start, middle and end of filling. The average is 100.52, the lowest 98.6. It seems to pass.
Then she puts her 100 gram test weight on the scale. It reads 101.
So the true average is 99.52 grams, and the lowest pouch is 97.6. Both rules fail.
She holds the batch, recalibrates, tops up every pouch below 100 grams, raises her fill target to 101, and records it all.
Never use a product pack as a test weight. Its true weight is exactly what you are trying to find out.

Training
The skills matrix levels
0: not trained
1: works only under supervision
2: signed off, works alone to standard
3: can train others
A skills matrix lists people down the side and tasks across the top. 0 means not trained.
1 means trained, but works only under supervision.
2 means signed off, working alone to standard.
3 means she can train others. Aim for at least two people at level 2 on every critical task, so one person's illness never stops production.
Worked example
Signing Amina off on handles
Rule: 3 batches of 10 in a row
No more than 1 rework per batch
Batch 1: 3 reworks, count restarts
Batches 2 to 4: 1, 0 and 1. Signed off
Sign off on numbers, not feelings.
For example, Chioma's sign-off rule for handles is three batches of 10 bags in a row. Handles must be 60 cm, plus or minus 1 cm.
Each batch may have no more than 1 bag needing rework.
Amina's first batch has 3 reworks. That is 30%, so the count restarts.
Her next three batches have 1, 0 and 1. Chioma signs and dates the matrix, moving her to level 2, with a refresher check in three months.
Decide the rule before training starts, so it is fair, and Amina can see the evidence herself.

Three rules for your team
Sign off hot oil, cutting tools, machines and chemicals first. Know the lid, first aid box and exit.
If anything does not match the spec, stop, set it aside and tell me. No blame for stopping.
An entry made from memory is not evidence. Fill in records as the work happens.
Train and sign off the safety steps before production steps. A learner should know where the lid, first aid box and exit are before she touches the pot.

Say this often. If anything does not match the spec, stop, set it aside and tell me. You will never be blamed for stopping. If people fear blame, they hide problems, and hidden problems reach customers.
And teach why each record matters. An entry made from memory is not evidence.
